code.title: Record basics and the shallow-immutability trap

followUps:
Records serialize by their components only, and deserialization calls the canonical constructor instead of bypassing constructors.

A normal Serializable class is rebuilt by writing fields straight into a fresh object, skipping the constructor. A record cannot be tampered with that way: the stream's component values are passed to the constructor, so your validation runs again. Custom writeObject/readObject methods are ignored and serialVersionUID is 0L unless declared.

The bytecode does not contain hand-written equals code; javac emits an invokedynamic call.

At first call the JVM runs the bootstrap method ObjectMethods.bootstrap, which builds method handles that compare each component (primitives by value, references with Objects.equals) and combines hashes. The bonus: the result is linked lazily and the class file stays small. For Point(1,2), equals compares x then y; hashCode combines 1 and 2 in an unspecified but consistent way.

Yes, a record can declare type parameters, for example record Pair<A, B>(A first, B second) {}.

Generics work as in classes: new Pair<>("a", 1) infers Pair<String,Integer>, and the accessors return the type variables. Record patterns can infer them too: case Pair(var f, var s). Erasure still applies, so at runtime a Pair has plain Object components.

code.title: Compact and delegating record constructors

followUps:
Because javac assigns the fields itself, after your body finishes, and allowing your own assignment would risk assigning twice or leaving a different value than the one validated.

In the compact form the parameters are the only thing you may change; the generated tail does this.lo = lo; this.hi = hi;. That guarantees every field is set exactly once and the stored value is the one you checked. If you need full control, write the long canonical constructor instead.

Records cannot have instance fields or constructors that skip the canonical one, but a static factory method can return cached instances.

record Color(int rgb) {
  private static final Map<Integer, Color> CACHE = new HashMap<>();
  static Color of(int rgb) {
    return CACHE.computeIfAbsent(rgb, Color::new);
  }
}

Use ConcurrentHashMap if threads share it, and remember the public constructor still exists unless you make the canonical one private.

code.title: Sealed interface with exhaustive switch

followUps:
Choose an enum when the variants are fixed constants with no per-instance data, and a sealed hierarchy when each variant carries different data.

An enum has one instance per constant (Color.RED); a sealed record such as Circle(double r) can have a million instances with different radii. Enums are better for serialization, EnumMap, values() and switch; sealed types are better when shapes differ. You can mix: a sealed interface implemented by an enum and by records.

The switch throws a MatchException, because the compiler-added default branch catches a subclass it never saw.

You compile switch(shape) with permitted types A and B. Later C is added to the interface and compiled separately, then C instances reach your old switch. No case matches, so the compiler's synthetic default throws. Fix: always rebuild consumers together.

If the sealed parent is a concrete class, it is itself a valid value, so a switch that only lists the subclasses is not exhaustive.

With sealed class Base permits A, B (not abstract), new Base() is legal, so you need a case Base b or default too. Make the parent an interface or an abstract class and the compiler accepts the switch with just A and B.

code.title: Pattern switch: guards, record patterns, null

followUps:
The exception propagates out of the switch wrapped in a MatchException, with the original as its cause.

Record patterns call accessor methods to deconstruct. If x() throws, say an ArithmeticException, the pattern match cannot continue, so javac's generated code wraps it: MatchException with getCause() being your exception. Plain accessors generated by the record never throw, so this only matters for hand-written ones.

Primitive patterns were deliberately left out of Java 21 because their meaning with conversions and boxing is subtle and needed their own design.

For example, should case int i match a Long, or a double 3.0 that converts exactly? They arrived later as a preview (JEP 455). In Java 21 you pattern-match on reference types and records, and use case Integer i for boxed values.

Java's pattern switch is closer to Scala's match than to Kotlin's when, but all three cover the same ground.

Kotlin when uses smart casts (is String -> s.length) and checks exhaustiveness over sealed types and enums. Scala has the richest patterns (extractors, nested, alternatives, guards with if). Java 21 added type, record and guard patterns with when, but no extractors or alternatives with bindings.

code.title: Text block stripping rules and escapes

followUps:
Use a backslash before one of the quotes: \""", or escape just enough so no three quotes appear in a row.

String s = """
    say \"""hi\"""
    """;

One or two plain quotes in a row are fine inside. Only a run of three closes the block, so escaping the first of them is enough.

Because formatted() only pastes text into the string, so a user-supplied value like ' OR '1'='1 becomes part of the SQL and enables SQL injection.

Use a PreparedStatement with ? placeholders: the text block holds the SQL with ?, and the driver sends values separately as data. A text block is excellent for readable SQL, but never for building it from input.

code.title: getMethods vs getDeclaredMethods and InvocationTargetException

followUps:
It is much faster than it used to be: since JDK 18 reflective calls are implemented with method handles, so they cost close to a normal call once warmed up.

Before JEP 416, the first 15 calls were native-code stubs and later ones generated bytecode accessors. Now Method.invoke uses direct method handles, which the JIT can inline when the method is a constant. It still boxes arguments and checks access, so a direct call can be a few times faster. Cache the Method object; the lookup is the costly part.

Because the Javadoc does not promise any order, and the JVM returns members in whatever order its internal tables hold them.

The order may differ between JDK versions, vendors or even runs after recompiling. Never rely on it: sort by name, or use an annotation or record component list (getRecordComponents() is ordered) when position matters. A serialization library that sorts fields explicitly avoids surprises.

code.title: Dynamic proxy and self-invocation bypass

followUps:
It is a checked exception thrown when a proxy method's handler throws a checked exception that the interface method does not declare.

Say the interface method declares no exceptions but your InvocationHandler throws IOException. The proxy cannot throw it, so it wraps it as UndeclaredThrowableException (an unchecked one) with the original as cause. Runtime exceptions and declared ones pass through unchanged.

Mockito generates a subclass of the class at runtime (using ByteBuddy) and overrides its methods to record calls and return stubbed values.

Modern Mockito's default inline mock maker instead instruments the class's bytecode through the Java agent API, so it can also mock final classes and static methods. Constructors are skipped via Objenesis so no real constructor code runs. Interfaces are just proxied.

code.title: Retention policies and repeatable annotations

followUps:
The compiler copies the annotation values from the record component to the places the annotation's @Target allows.

For record P(@NotNull String name), an annotation with FIELD target lands on the private field, METHOD on the accessor, PARAMETER on the canonical constructor parameter, and RECORD_COMPONENT on the component. If the target is none of these, it is a compile error. With no @Target, it applies to all that fit.

It is a generated proxy object implementing the annotation interface, backed by a map of the element values.

Calling tag.value() reads from the stored map, and toString, equals and hashCode are built from that map. The class name looks like jdk.proxy2.$Proxy1. Instances are cached per annotated element, so repeated lookups are cheap.

Generating code at compile time gives speed and early errors, while runtime reflection gives flexibility with less build setup.

Generated code has no reflection cost, works with GraalVM native image, and mistakes show up as compile errors (MapStruct mappers, Dagger graphs). The price is slower builds, harder debugging of generated sources and processor-version coupling. Reflection (Spring, Jackson) needs nothing special at build time but fails at runtime, is slower on startup and needs reachability hints for native images.

Use the compile-testing library, which compiles snippets in memory with your processor and lets you assert on the diagnostics and generated files.

Compilation c = javac()
  .withProcessors(new MyProcessor())
  .compile(JavaFileObjects.forSourceString("A", src));
assertThat(c).succeeded();
assertThat(c).generatedSourceFile("AGen");

Also test the error path: bad input should give a clear message at the right line.

jlink reads the module graph, finds every module your app transitively needs, and builds a small custom runtime containing only those.

Run jdeps or give --add-modules, and jlink resolves requires edges, then copies just those modules into an image. An app needing only java.base and java.sql may shrink from a 300 MB JDK to about 50 MB. It needs real modules: automatic modules and classpath-only jars block it.

Because many libraries are not modular yet, and the classpath just works without module descriptors, so the migration cost is not worth it for most applications.

The classpath puts everything in one unnamed module that reads everything, so no module-info.java and no split-package errors. Apps still benefit from the modular JDK underneath. Modules pay off mainly for libraries wanting strong encapsulation and for jlink-shrunk runtimes.

code.title: InaccessibleObjectException on JDK internals

followUps:
It lists which JDK internal packages your jars call, so you know what will break on a newer JDK.

Run jdeps --jdk-internals app.jar. Output lines look like Foo.class -> JDK internal API sun.misc.Unsafe, with a suggested replacement where one exists. Use --multi-release 17 for multi-release jars and run it on all dependency jars, since the culprit is usually a library, not your code.

The JDK is deprecating sun.misc.Unsafe's memory-access methods in steps, so each use gets a warning first and later throws.

Supported replacements exist: VarHandle for atomic and ordered field access, and the Foreign Function and Memory API (MemorySegment) for off-heap memory with bounds checking. JEP 471 deprecates the methods for removal; JEP 498 makes the JVM warn at the first use. Libraries like Netty and Kryo have been moving to the new APIs.

code.title: Benchmark skeleton: warm-up, sink, repeats

followUps:
OSR means on-stack replacement: the JIT swaps a running loop's interpreted code for compiled code mid-execution, and a benchmark in main can be measured in that unusual state.

A hot loop in main only runs once, so the JVM compiles it through OSR, which can be less optimized than a normal compile of a method called many times. JMH calls the benchmark method repeatedly in fresh forks, so you measure the normal compiled version.

Use SingleShotTime when you want the cost of one cold call, such as application startup, first request or class loading, not steady state.

It runs the method once per iteration with no warm-up loop inside. Typical cases: how long a CLI takes to start, or the first parse of a config file. Run many forks to get a distribution, since one cold sample varies a lot.

Add a benchmark job that stores results per commit and fails the build when a key benchmark gets slower than a threshold, compared with a stable baseline.

Run JMH on dedicated, quiet hardware, with fixed CPU frequency, several forks, and compare confidence intervals, not single numbers (for example, fail only on a regression above 10% outside the error bars). Track allocation too with -prof gc. Add canary and p99 latency alerts in production as a second net.

CPU limits throttle the process in time slices, so a container may stop running for milliseconds even if the host is idle, which adds noise and inflates tail latency.

A limit of 1 CPU on a 16-core host also changes what the JVM sees: it may size GC threads and the JIT compiler pool from the limit, not the host. Benchmark on the same limits as production, repeat runs, and compare p99, not only the mean.

code.title: Integer cache and == pitfalls

followUps:
Wrappers Byte, Short, Long, Character and Boolean cache values, but Float and Double do not.

Byte caches all 256 values, Short and Long cache -128..127, Character caches 0..127, and Boolean has just TRUE and FALSE. Double.valueOf(1.0) == Double.valueOf(1.0) is false. In all cases compare with equals.

Value classes (Project Valhalla) are meant to have no identity, so == on them would compare field values, like a primitive.

That would make Integer a value class eventually, so Integer a = 128, b = 128; a == b could be true. Until that ships, treat == on wrappers as an identity comparison, and write code with equals that stays correct either way.

code.title: Class and object initialization order

followUps:
It is thread-safe because the JVM initializes a class once, under a lock, the first time it is used, and the holder class is only used when getInstance() is first called.

class S {
  private static class H { static final S I = new S(); }
  static S get() { return H.I; }
}

Initialization is lazy (nothing is built until get()) and no synchronized is needed on later calls, because the class is already initialized.

A constant variable is a final variable of primitive or String type, initialized with a compile-time constant expression.

static final int MAX = 10; and final String S = "a" + "b"; qualify; static final Integer N = 10; does not (not primitive/String) and neither does final int x = f();. The compiler inlines constants into callers, so reading them does not trigger class initialization.

code.title: Sealed switch vs open polymorphism

followUps:
Keep the hierarchy additive: only add permitted types in a compatible way and tell clients up front that switches need a default.

Adding a permitted subtype breaks exhaustive switches in client code on recompile, and throws MatchException if they do not. Options: expose the sealed type only for output (clients read, never implement), add a default branch in your docs' examples, or version the API with a new interface. Removing a subtype is always breaking.

Data-oriented programming means modelling data as plain immutable records in sealed hierarchies and writing logic as separate functions over them; records are the data half.

A sealed interface Event with record cases is the data; handle(Event e) is a switch elsewhere. Records give value equality and deconstruction, sealed gives a closed set. Use it for data that crosses boundaries (messages, results) and keep behaviour with objects where state matters.

code.title: Sequenced collections in Java 21

followUps:
It is a live view: reversed() shows the same elements in opposite order without copying them.

If you add 5 to the original list, the reversed view shows it at the front, as my demo printed. Writes through the view (like addFirst on it) change the original too. Cost is O(1) to create, no extra storage. Copy it with new ArrayList<>(list.reversed()) if you need a snapshot.

It throws UnsupportedOperationException, because List.of is unmodifiable and all mutating methods, including the new ones, are rejected.

List.of(1,2).addFirst(0) fails even though it is just inserting at the start. The same goes for removeFirst on such a list, and for Collections.unmodifiableList wrappers. Read methods like getFirst() work, and throw NoSuchElementException only when the list is empty.
